name: Why a Teacher Reads First
title: Why a Teacher Reads First
answer: Every AI tool that produces perspectives, summaries, or historical content should be read by a teacher before students see it. The reason is that these tools learn from huge amounts of human writing, and that writing carries the blind spots and biases of its authors. A teacher's quick review catches stereotypes, missing viewpoints, and one sided framing before they shape how students understand people and events.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: AI tools are trained on enormous quantities of text written by people, so they absorb the biases and blind spots of those authors. In practice this means a tool may describe a group in a stereotyped way, leave a group out altogether, or present one side of a contested question as though it were settled fact. In social studies this matters more than almost anywhere else, because the output can shape how students understand whole peoples and historical events. A tool asked about a historical conflict may favor whichever side left more published records, and a tool asked about a religion or culture may repeat outdated or offensive ideas. Students are unlikely to spot these problems on their own, particularly when the writing sounds authoritative.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The teacher reads the tool's output first, before it reaches students, and the review does not need to take long. A quick read is enough to look for stereotypes, missing perspectives, one sided framing, and claims that need checking, and Figure 9.4 sets out what to look for. The supplied text does not assign this practice to particular grade bands, so it is described as a general step for any classroom using these tools. When the teacher does find a problem, that problem can become a lesson in itself. Students can then be taught to read AI output with the same care they would bring to any other source.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text points to one study, cited as Liang et al., 2023 and described in Chapter 1, which found that bias in AI detectors wrongly flagged writing by students learning English. That is the only research finding the text offers, and it concerns AI detectors rather than the social studies tools discussed here. The rest of the guidance, including the teacher's pre reading of output and the checklist in Figure 9.4, rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the teacher's judgement is the safeguard, and that this step cannot be handed to the tool itself. The risks it names are stereotyped descriptions of groups, groups left out entirely, one side of a contested issue presented as settled fact, and claims that need checking. Students may not recognize any of these, especially when the text sounds authoritative, which is why the reading happens before they see it. The decision about what is acceptable for a given class stays with the teacher, and a problem found in the output is treated as something to teach from rather than something to quietly delete.
